## Two chords decide how a phrase signs off

Hold five chords of harmony completely still and change only the two that follow.
V to I reaches home with pressure behind it. IV to I gets there more gently. A
phrase that stops on V stays open. V to vi aims straight at the tonic and then
steps aside at the last moment. Same phrase, four different pieces of
punctuation.

A *cadence* is a conventional harmonic gesture at a phrase boundary, and those
four behaviours are called authentic, plagal, half and deceptive. Learn the
names next to the sounds they organise. A cadence isn't a two-chord arrow on a
page; it's what that arrow does once enough context has made a boundary
audible in the first place.

## Four endings on one body

The chords below are written out as MIDI numbers rather than produced by
`chord()`, and that matters. Each one holds a common tone where the harmony
offers one and moves the remaining voices by step, and all four sit in the same
register, so nothing arrives by jumping an octave. [Lesson 31](31-voice-leading-optimisation-problem.qmd) is where you learn
to search for voicings like these; here they're hand-written so the comparison
stays clean.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 88
use_synth :piano

# bass / tenor / alto / soprano, all four chords in one register
voicings = {
  I: [48, 64, 67, 72],    # C3 E4 G4 C5
  IV: [53, 65, 69, 72],   # F3 F4 A4 C5
  V: [55, 62, 67, 71],    # G3 D4 G4 B4
  vi: [57, 60, 64, 72]    # A3 C4 E4 C5
}

define :play_cadence_phrase do |voicings, ending|
  body = [:I, :vi, :IV, :V, :I]
  (body + ending).each do |name|
    play_chord voicings[name], release: 1.7
    sleep 2
  end
end

endings = {
  authentic: [:V, :I],
  plagal: [:IV, :I],
  half: [:IV, :V],
  deceptive: [:V, :vi]
}

endings.each do |name, ending|
  puts name
  play_cadence_phrase voicings, ending
  sleep 2
end
```

Every run ends its body on the same tonic chord, so all four endings start from
identical sound and only the last two chords differ. Authentic and plagal both
reach I, but V carries the leading tone B and pushes forward harder than IV
does. The half cadence stops on that push and leaves it unspent. The deceptive
ending goes to vi, and because I and vi share C and E, the substitution feels
connected even as the destination slips away.

Notice that the soprano barely moves: C5 for every chord except V. That's
deliberate. With no tune on top to carry the ending, whatever you hear as
closure has to be coming from the harmony underneath.

## Weaken each cue in turn

1. Delete the body and play each two-chord ending on its own. The pairs are
   still different, but their cadential identity thins out, because there's less
   phrase for them to complete or interrupt.

2. Hold the final chord for four beats. Extra length gives every boundary more
   authority. It still can't supply the tonic that a half cadence never reaches.

3. Replace the final `I` with `[52, 64, 67, 72]`, putting E in the bass. The
   label is still V-I, and the landing is softer. How much of "arrival" was the
   root under the chord rather than the chord itself?

## What each approach chord actually does

V contains B, one semitone under C. Add F and you get V7, which puts two active
tones in play at once: B pulls up to C while F pulls down to E. IV reaches the
tonic through a different pair of short moves, F to E and A to G, with no
leading tone anywhere in it. Both cadences travel small distances. What differs
is what the approach chord was straining toward.

A half cadence stops after the directional harmony has spoken. V will support a
pause, and it still predicts continuation, which is exactly why a phrase can
rest there without sounding finished. The deceptive cadence turns that
prediction against you. You expect C-E-G and you get A-C-E: two of the three
promised tones arrive on schedule, and a new bass note reinterprets both of them
as vi.

Because each ending is a two-symbol suffix on shared body data, the comparison
is honest. The renderer has no instruction to sound conclusive or evasive. It
plays the named chords, and their order acquires meaning from the tonal context
set up beforehand.

Melody can back the harmony up or fight it. A final C over the tonic lines up
bass, harmony and melodic goal. An E lets the harmony close while the top voice
stays unrooted, and a G leaves it more open still. Cadence names describe a
harmonic skeleton, not everything a listener hears at the end of a phrase.

Timing shifts the result too. Silence after V lets a half cadence register as a
deliberate question. Run straight on and the same chord becomes a connector.
Keep pauses and durations fixed for the four-way test, then vary them once a
timing cue won't be mistaken for a new cadence type.

## Build the confusion table

Make a ten-trial drill from the four endings. Start with `use_random_seed 42`,
pick an ending, play the body and the cadence, leave four beats for your answer,
then print the name. Hold voicing, duration, synth and pause length constant
across every trial.

Record your errors by pair, not as a single score. Authentic against plagal and
half against deceptive are the two confusions worth counting: one asks which
chord approached the tonic, the other asks whether the tonic arrived at all.
Whichever pair you miss more is the one to slow down and run again.
